## Construction and selection of Bayesian C and d14C models

Eight separate regularised Bayesian multiple-regression models were developed to investigate relationships between soil geochemical properties and carbon (C) and radiocarbon (d14C) responses in bulk soil, mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM), occluded particulate organic matter (oPOM), and free particulate organic matter (fPOM). The response variables comprised C_Bulk, C_MAOM, C_oPOM, C_fPOM and their corresponding 2026 d14C values.

Candidate explanatory variables included soil chemical properties, aggregate stability indices, exchangeable and reducible cation fractions, oxalate-extractable mineral ratios, and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectral changes. Predictors were retained when at least 70% of observations were available. Remaining missing predictor values were imputed using the respective predictor median. Predictors exhibiting no variation were removed, and severe predictor multicollinearity was reduced by iteratively excluding one variable from predictor pairs with an absolute Pearson correlation coefficient exceeding 0.95. All predictors and response variables were standardised prior to model fitting.

The full reference models were specified as Gaussian multiple-regression models in Stan. The intercept was assigned a Normal(0, 1) prior, regression coefficients were assigned regularising Normal(0, 0.5) priors, and the residual standard deviation was assigned an exponential prior with rate 1. Models were fitted using four Markov chain Monte Carlo chains through CmdStanR, with 1,500 warm-up iterations and 2,000 retained sampling iterations per chain. Convergence was assessed using the potential scale reduction factor (R-hat), effective sample sizes, divergent transitions, and posterior predictive checks.

### Projection predictive variable selection and model parsimony

Projection predictive variable selection was conducted using the `projpred` package. The full reference model posterior was used as the reference distribution for identifying reduced predictor combinations. A forward-search procedure evaluated increasingly complex submodels, with a maximum of five predictors considered. The predictive performance of candidate submodels was assessed using the projection predictive validation procedure.

To balance predictive performance and model complexity, the most parsimonious candidate model was selected using the one-standard-error (1-SE) criterion. Specifically, the smallest candidate submodel whose predictive performance was within one standard error of the best-performing candidate was retained. This approach favours a simpler model when the improvement in predictive performance from including additional predictors is not sufficiently substantial to justify the increased model complexity.

The selected predictor combination was subsequently refitted as an independent Bayesian Gaussian regression model using the same standardisation procedures, regularising priors, and MCMC settings as the reference model. Thus, posterior coefficient estimates and fitted predictions presented here originate from the refitted selected model rather than directly from the projection step.

### Interpretation of predictions and predictor importance

Observed-versus-predicted plots display posterior mean fitted values together with 95% credible intervals for the fitted mean and 95% posterior predictive intervals. The shaded regions represent uncertainty in the estimated conditional mean, whereas the error bars represent the wider uncertainty associated with individual posterior predictive observations. Predictions are in-sample fitted predictions and should not be interpreted as independent external validation.

Relative predictor importance was calculated using the absolute posterior mean standardised regression coefficients. For each selected model, the absolute coefficient of each predictor was divided by the sum of the absolute coefficients of all included predictors and multiplied by 100. Consequently, relative importance percentages sum to 100% within each model. These values provide a measure of the relative magnitude of conditional standardised associations and do not represent independent variance explained or causal contributions.

Because the predictors and responses were standardised, regression coefficients describe the expected change in the standardised response associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in a predictor, conditional on the other selected predictors. Coefficient direction and uncertainty should therefore be considered alongside relative importance when interpreting the relationships.

## Load selected best-model predictions and coefficients

This document is plot-only. It loads the prediction and coefficient CSV files saved by the model-fitting script. No Bayesian models are refitted and no new variable-selection procedure is performed here.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(patchwork)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Output directories
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

out_dir <- here::here(
  "outputs",
  "bayesian_C_d14C_predictions_withftir"
)

table_dir <- file.path(out_dir, "tables")
plot_dir <- file.path(out_dir, "plots")

if (!dir.exists(table_dir)) {
  stop("Table directory does not exist: ", table_dir)
}

dir.create(
  plot_dir,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Expected responses
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

responses <- c(
  "C_Bulk",
  "C_MAOM",
  "C_oPOM",
  "C_fPOM",
  "d14C_2026_Bulk",
  "d14C_2026_MAOM",
  "d14C_2026_oPOM",
  "d14C_2026_fPOM"
)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Filename helpers
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

safe_name <- function(x) {
  x %>%
    stringr::str_replace_all("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_") %>%
    stringr::str_replace_all("^_|_$", "")
}

best_prediction_file <- function(response) {
  file.path(
    table_dir,
    paste0(
      "predictions_",
      safe_name(response),
      "__bestmod.csv"
    )
  )
}

best_coefficient_file <- function(response) {
  file.path(
    table_dir,
    paste0(
      "coefficients_",
      safe_name(response),
      "__bestmod.csv"
    )
  )
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Check available best-model outputs
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

prediction_files <- setNames(
  map_chr(responses, best_prediction_file),
  responses
)

coefficient_files <- setNames(
  map_chr(responses, best_coefficient_file),
  responses
)

available_responses <- responses[
  file.exists(prediction_files)
]

if (length(available_responses) == 0L) {
  stop(
    "No best-model prediction CSVs were found.\n",
    "Expected files such as:\n",
    "predictions_C_Bulk__bestmod.csv\n",
    "in: ", table_dir,
    "\nRun the updated Bayesian model-fitting script first."
  )
}

missing_predictions <- setdiff(
  responses,
  available_responses
)

if (length(missing_predictions) > 0L) {
  message(
    "Best-model predictions unavailable for: ",
    paste(missing_predictions, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

available_coefficient_responses <- responses[
  file.exists(coefficient_files)
]

missing_coefficients <- setdiff(
  available_responses,
  available_coefficient_responses
)

if (length(missing_coefficients) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "Best-model coefficient CSVs are missing for: ",
    paste(missing_coefficients, collapse = ", "),
    "\nBoth prediction and coefficient CSVs are required ",
    "to generate the combined plots."
  )
}

message(
  "Best models available for ",
  length(available_responses),
  " responses."
)

message(
  "Plot output directory: ",
  plot_dir
)
```

## Relative predictor importance

The relative importance of each predictor is calculated from the absolute posterior mean standardised regression coefficients of the selected model.

```{r}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Identify predictor and coefficient columns
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

identify_predictor_column <- function(coef_tbl) {

  possible_columns <- c(
    "term",
    "Predictor",
    "predictor",
    "variable",
    "Variable"
  )

  found <- possible_columns[
    possible_columns %in% names(coef_tbl)
  ]

  if (length(found) == 0L) {
    stop(
      "Could not identify predictor column. Available columns: ",
      paste(names(coef_tbl), collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  found[1]
}


identify_standardised_coefficient_column <- function(coef_tbl) {

  # The fitting script stores posterior mean coefficients
  # in Estimate, estimated on standardised predictor and
  # standardised response scales.

  possible_columns <- c(
    "Estimate",
    "mean_standardized",
    "mean_standardised",
    "mean_std",
    "beta_std"
  )

  found <- possible_columns[
    possible_columns %in% names(coef_tbl)
  ]

  if (length(found) == 0L) {
    stop(
      "Could not identify standardised coefficient column. ",
      "Available columns: ",
      paste(names(coef_tbl), collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  found[1]
}


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate relative importance
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

calculate_relative_importance <- function(coef_tbl, response) {

  predictor_col <- identify_predictor_column(coef_tbl)

  coefficient_col <- identify_standardised_coefficient_column(
    coef_tbl
  )

  importance_tbl <- coef_tbl %>%
    transmute(
      Predictor = as.character(.data[[predictor_col]]),
      Standardised_coefficient = as.numeric(
        .data[[coefficient_col]]
      )
    ) %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(Predictor),
      is.finite(Standardised_coefficient)
    ) %>%
    filter(
      !str_detect(
        tolower(Predictor),
        "intercept|^alpha$|^sigma$|residual|^lp__$"
      )
    )

  if (nrow(importance_tbl) == 0L) {
    stop(
      "No predictor coefficients found for ",
      response
    )
  }

  total_absolute_coefficient <- sum(
    abs(importance_tbl$Standardised_coefficient)
  )

  if (
    !is.finite(total_absolute_coefficient) ||
    total_absolute_coefficient <= 0
  ) {
    stop(
      "Invalid total absolute coefficient magnitude for ",
      response
    )
  }

  importance_tbl %>%
    mutate(
      Relative_importance =
        abs(Standardised_coefficient) /
        total_absolute_coefficient * 100
    ) %>%
    arrange(Relative_importance) %>%
    mutate(
      Predictor = factor(
        Predictor,
        levels = Predictor
      )
    )
}

```

## Observed-versus-predicted plots of selected best models

The upper panel displays observed versus posterior mean predicted values, including the 95% credible ribbon and 95% posterior predictive intervals. The lower panel displays the relative importance of the predictors retained in the selected model.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: 95%
#| dpi: 160

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Upper panel: observed versus predicted
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

plot_observed_predicted_bestmod <- function(
    pred,
    response
) {

  required <- c(
    "observed",
    "predicted_mean",
    "fitted_lower_95",
    "fitted_upper_95",
    "predictive_lower_95",
    "predictive_upper_95",
    "Treatment_model"
  )

  absent <- setdiff(
    required,
    names(pred)
  )

  if (length(absent) > 0L) {
    stop(
      "Missing prediction columns for ",
      response,
      ": ",
      paste(absent, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  pred <- pred %>%
    filter(
      is.finite(observed),
      is.finite(predicted_mean)
    ) %>%
    arrange(observed) %>%
    mutate(
      Treatment_model = factor(Treatment_model)
    )

  if (nrow(pred) == 0L) {
    stop("No valid prediction observations for ", response)
  }

  model_size <- if ("n_predictors" %in% names(pred)) {
    unique(pred$n_predictors)[1]
  } else {
    NA_integer_
  }

  model_subtitle <- if (is.finite(model_size)) {
    paste0(
      "Projpred-selected best model (",
      model_size,
      " predictors)"
    )
  } else {
    "Projpred-selected best model"
  }

  ggplot(
    pred,
    aes(
      x = observed,
      y = predicted_mean
    )
  ) +

    geom_ribbon(
      aes(
        ymin = fitted_lower_95,
        ymax = fitted_upper_95
      ),
      fill = "grey70",
      alpha = 0.55
    ) +

    geom_errorbar(
      aes(
        ymin = predictive_lower_95,
        ymax = predictive_upper_95
      ),
      width = 0,
      alpha = 0.35,
      colour = "grey40"
    ) +

    geom_point(
      aes(shape = Treatment_model),
      size = 2.8,
      alpha = 0.9
    ) +

    geom_abline(
      intercept = 0,
      slope = 1,
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.7,
      colour = "black"
    ) +

    coord_equal() +

    labs(
      title = paste(
        "Observed vs Bayesian predicted:",
        response
      ),
      subtitle = paste0(
        model_subtitle,
        " | Shaded band = 95% credible interval for fitted mean; ",
        "whiskers = 95% posterior predictive interval"
      ),
      x = paste("Observed", response),
      y = paste("Predicted", response),
      shape = "Treatment"
    ) +

    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +

    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Lower panel: relative predictor importance
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

plot_relative_importance_bestmod <- function(
    importance_tbl,
    response
) {

  n_predictors <- nrow(importance_tbl)

  ggplot(
    importance_tbl,
    aes(
      x = Relative_importance,
      y = Predictor
    )
  ) +

    geom_col(
      fill = "#2878B5",
      width = 0.72,
      alpha = 0.9
    ) +

    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = sprintf(
          "%.1f%%",
          Relative_importance
        )
      ),
      hjust = -0.15,
      size = 3.2
    ) +

    scale_x_continuous(
      limits = c(
        0,
        max(importance_tbl$Relative_importance) * 1.20
      ),
      expand = expansion(
        mult = c(0, 0.02)
      )
    ) +

    labs(
      title = "Relative importance of selected predictors",
      subtitle = paste0(
        "Absolute standardised posterior mean coefficients; ",
        n_predictors,
        " predictors normalised to sum to 100%"
      ),
      x = "Relative importance (%)",
      y = NULL
    ) +

    theme_bw(base_size = 10) +

    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        size = 11
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8.5),
      axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.5),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.margin = margin(
        t = 5,
        r = 25,
        b = 5,
        l = 5
      )
    )
}


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Generate all selected best-model plots
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

best_model_plot_list <- list()

for (response in available_responses) {

  message(
    "\nGenerating best-model plot for: ",
    response
  )

  # Load predictions
  pred <- readr::read_csv(
    best_prediction_file(response),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  # Load coefficients
  coef_tbl <- readr::read_csv(
    best_coefficient_file(response),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  # Calculate relative importance
  importance_tbl <- calculate_relative_importance(
    coef_tbl,
    response
  )

  # Generate upper panel
  observed_plot <- plot_observed_predicted_bestmod(
    pred,
    response
  )

  # Generate lower panel
  importance_plot <- plot_relative_importance_bestmod(
    importance_tbl,
    response
  )

  # Combine panels
  combined_plot <- observed_plot /
    importance_plot +

    plot_layout(
      heights = c(
        3,
        max(1.1, 0.20 * nrow(importance_tbl))
      )
    ) +

    plot_annotation(
      caption = paste0(
        "Relative importance is calculated from absolute posterior ",
        "mean standardised coefficients. Percentages sum to 100% ",
        "within each selected model and do not represent variance ",
        "explained or causal contributions."
      ),
      theme = theme(
        plot.caption = element_text(
          size = 8,
          colour = "grey35",
          hjust = 0
        )
      )
    )

  # Display in rendered HTML
  print(combined_plot)

  # Save plot
  output_file <- file.path(
    plot_dir,
    paste0(
      "Observed_vs_Predicted_with_Relative_Importance_",
      safe_name(response),
      "_bestmod.png"
    )
  )

  output_height <- max(
    8,
    6.2 + 0.20 * nrow(importance_tbl)
  )

  ggsave(
    filename = output_file,
    plot = combined_plot,
    width = 10,
    height = output_height,
    dpi = 320,
    limitsize = FALSE,
    bg = "white"
  )

  best_model_plot_list[[response]] <- combined_plot

  message(
    "Saved: ",
    output_file
  )
}

```

## Best-model plot summary

```{r}
plot_summary <- tibble(
  response = available_responses,
  prediction_file = map_chr(
    available_responses,
    best_prediction_file
  ),
  coefficient_file = map_chr(
    available_responses,
    best_coefficient_file
  ),
  plot_file = map_chr(
    available_responses,
    ~ file.path(

    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  plot_summary,
  caption = "Generated observed-versus-predicted plots for the selected best models",
  format = "html"
)

```

## Interpretation and limitations

The selected models provide a parsimonious representation of the relationships between soil geochemical properties and carbon and radiocarbon responses. Predictor importance should be interpreted in conjunction with coefficient direction, posterior uncertainty, and the underlying soil processes.

The one-standard-error selection criterion favours reduced model complexity when additional predictors provide limited improvements in predictive performance. Nevertheless, the selected models represent conditional statistical associations and do not independently establish causal mechanisms.

The observed-versus-predicted plots are based on the observations used to fit the selected models. Accordingly, their agreement with observed values should not be interpreted as an unbiased estimate of out-of-sample predictive accuracy. The projection predictive validation results should be used when discussing predictive performance and model selection.

```

## Important before rendering

There are two things to ensure in the model-fitting script:

- It must actually apply the 1-SE parsimony rule when choosing the best model, rather than simply choosing the three-predictor model or automatically using five predictors.
- It must save the selected model's predictions and coefficients using the `__bestmod.csv` naming convention above.

The QMD deliberately does not perform model selection again: it only visualises the saved, selected models. This keeps model fitting and figure generation separate and reproducible.
